articles.title: I make my launch videos with a web page, not a video editor
articles.excerpt: I don't know Premiere. I didn't want to learn it just to make a 30-second trailer for a side project. So I made the video a web page instead. The whole trailer is one 1920x1080 page where everything o…
articles.body: I don't know Premiere. I didn't want to learn it just to make a 30-second trailer for a side project. So I made the video a web page instead. The idea The whole trailer is one 1920x1080 page where everything on screen is a pure function of time. No timers, no animation libraries, no Math.random() while rendering. You give the page a time t , and it draws exactly what frame t should look like. I expose one hook on the page, window.__trailer.seek(t) . It sets the state, pauses every CSS animation and sets its currentTime from t , waits for images to decode, then waits two animation frames so the paint is done. Rendering A Playwright script opens the page, and for every frame i it calls seek(i / 30) and takes a screenshot.
articles.author: Susan Acharya

articles.title: Nobody clicks "click here": a small Python check for vague link text
articles.excerpt: Link text is one of those things I never thought about until I started paying attention to how people actually move through a page. Most readers don't read every word. They scan, and links stand out b…
articles.body: Link text is one of those things I never thought about until I started paying attention to how people actually move through a page. Most readers don't read every word. They scan, and links stand out because they look different from everything around them. If the highlighted words are "click here" or "read more", the scan tells them nothing. It matters even more for people using a screen reader. Many screen readers can list all the links on a page so you can jump straight to the one you want. A list that says "here, here, read more, this, here" is useless. A list that says "keyboard shortcut cheat sheet, style guide, accessibility checklist" works without any surrounding text at all. So I made a rule for myself: every link should make sense if you read only the linked words.

articles.title: The code was done. The four announcements weren't.
articles.excerpt: You finish the update. Then you open Telegram, X, DEV and GitHub, and discover that you have four more things to write. The facts haven't changed. The readers have. Telegram wants the update without a…
articles.body: You finish the update. Then you open Telegram, X, DEV and GitHub, and discover that you have four more things to write. The facts haven't changed. The readers have. Telegram wants the update without a long introduction. X gives you one small patch of screen. DEV needs a reason to keep reading. GitHub needs the concrete details someone will look for later. That's the gap I'm building PatchPitch for: keep the facts in one place, then prepare drafts for each audience. For 0.3.0, currently in development, I wanted the whole job to run from the command line. A writing tool that needs someone to babysit a browser leaves a rather large hole in the automation. The result: four local drafts in 123.258 seconds, using five requests to a local Ollama model.

articles.title: Why Your AI Agent Sent That Message Twice, and What to Require Before Launch
articles.excerpt: Your AI agent sent the message twice because something underneath it retried, not because the model "decided" to. Webhooks, queues, workers and LLM API clients all default to at-least-once delivery, a…
articles.body: Your AI agent sent the message twice because something underneath it retried, not because the model "decided" to. Webhooks, queues, workers and LLM API clients all default to at-least-once delivery, and an agent that calls the outside world without an idempotency key will eventually double-send, double-book or double-charge. The fix is architectural and cheap compared to the damage, so it belongs in the requirements, not in a post-launch patch. Retries are the default, not the exception Founders tend to picture an agent as a single conversation: a customer writes, the model thinks, a reply goes out. In production it is a chain of hops, and nearly every hop will repeat itself under stress. The inbound webhook.

articles.title: SimpleStart: Build Interactive Web Apps in Pure Python
articles.excerpt: Every Python programmer eventually hits the same wall: the script works, but you want colleagues without a Python environment to use it — which means it needs a web page. Suddenly you're facing HTML,…
articles.body: Every Python programmer eventually hits the same wall: the script works, but you want colleagues without a Python environment to use it — which means it needs a web page. Suddenly you're facing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, maybe npm and a build toolchain. Most people stop at that wall: the tool stays a command-line script, or a CSV gets emailed around instead. SimpleStart is one answer to that wall: a pure-Python web framework. You write Python scripts; it renders the UI in the browser. For most scenarios you never touch HTML/CSS/JS — no node, no npm, no bundler. And when you truly need fine control, there are escape hatches ( ss.css for styles, ss.loadvue for custom components — covered below).

articles.excerpt: The full-scale prototype of Europe's Space Rider orbiter failed to deploy its parachute during a drop test earlier this month, but ESA officials hope the setback won't delay progress toward its first…
articles.body: Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 22, 1992: Ashes of 'Star Trek' creator Gene Roddenberry launch into space on NASA shuttle
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of "Star Trek." Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight.

articles.title: After Starshield interruption, Ukraine wants to build its own satellite communication network with ICEYE and Nokia
articles.excerpt: Ukraine's military just signed a letter of intent with Nokia and the Finnish satellite maker ICEYE to look into developing a sovereign satellite-communication system for the war-torn nation.
articles.body: Ukraine wants its own satellite-communication system, which shouldn't be surprising given the events of the past week or so. The Ukrainian military just signed a letter of intent with two Finnish companies — the telecom giant Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE — to look into developing a sovereign satellite-communications network for Ukraine. "Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," ICEYE cofounder and CEO Rafal Modrzewski said in a statement today (Oct. 22). "We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability.

articles.body: Right now, there is probably an AI agent running on a laptop somewhere in your network. It stores API keys and database passwords, can access your internal systems, and works without anyone watching. Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it.
